title: Prompt-to-Task Workshop (Lab)
summary: Students tackle a richer multi-requirement task with two different prompt structures, compare them on completion and accuracy, and turn the stronger one into a reusable template with a verification step and risk check built in.
objectives: Complete a second, richer task and compare which prompt structure worked better.
Design a reusable prompt structure for a class of tasks.
Evaluate the outputs for accuracy and run a basic risk check.

sections.heading: Prompt-to-Task Workshop (Lab)
body: You can structure one prompt - now build something reusable. Today you compare prompt structures on a richer task and design a template you and your class can use again and again.

sections.heading: I can…
items: I can complete a richer task with a structured prompt and compare two structures.
I can design a reusable prompt template for similar tasks.
I can check an output for accuracy and complete a risk check.

terms.definition: A task with several requirements to complete.
The order and parts of a prompt, such as Goal-Context-Format.
A prompt skeleton with slots that works for many similar tasks.
Checking an output against a reliable source.
A quick check for personal data and possible errors.

sections.heading: Compare, then reuse
body: A [[richer task]] has several requirements, so a weak prompt structure leaves parts unfinished. Run two structures on the same task and compare which completes it and which is more accurate.
Then turn the winner into a [[reusable template]] - a prompt with labelled slots you can fill in for any similar task.

sections.heading: Build in the checks
body: Every good template forces two checks: verify the output against a reliable source, and run a [[risk check]] for personal data and errors.
This is how real AI solutions are designed - and it is the foundation for your signature activity in the coming weeks.

sections.label: Let's try it - hands-on
sections.heading: Let's try it - hands-on
body: Complete a richer task with two structures, compare them, then design a reusable template with checks built in.
items: List the three requirements of the task.
Draft two structured prompts with different orders.
Compare which output completed the task and check accuracy.
Turn the stronger structure into a reusable template.
Add a verification step and a risk check.

sections.heading: Think about it
items: Which structure completed more of the task, and how do you know?
Where should the verify step sit in your template?

sections.heading: My reflection
items: Write the biggest difference between your two structures.
Write how your template forces an accuracy check.

questions.stem:
Structure A met ___ of 3
Structure B met ___ of 3
The stronger structure was ___ because ___
questions.lookFor: The comparison must be on completion or accuracy, not length - for example 'Structure A met all three requirements; Structure B missed the tone, so A was stronger.' Emerging (expected): compares two structures on completion and accuracy with evidence. Watch for the misconception that the longest answer is the best.

questions.stem:
Goal: ___
Context (no personal data): ___
Format: ___
Verify: ___
questions.lookFor: Model template: 'Goal: [task]; Context: [details, no personal data]; Format: [exact format]; then Verify: check facts against a source.' The template must include a verify/risk step and use labelled slots rather than one fixed task. Emerging (expected): a clear reusable template with labelled slots.

Evidence for the comparison: both structures recorded, requirements met marked per structure, an accuracy check against a reliable source, and a stated winner. A record that marks completion but never checks accuracy is only approaching - sounding right is not being right.

questions.stem: Write your reusable template in one line and say how it checks accuracy.
questions.lookFor: A one-line template with labelled slots (Goal / Context / Format) plus a named verification step - checking the output against a reliable source before use. Privacy (no personal data requested) is a bonus here; both privacy and accuracy must appear in the risk check overall.

questions.stem: Test your template on a genuinely different task and note where it needed changing.
questions.lookFor: Stretch task: groups test the template on a genuinely different task type and report where it needed changing. Look for the insight that a template is a strong starting point, not a guarantee - each new task still needs its output verified.
